issues.subcategory: placeholder manuscript based on dummy data
issues.description: The manuscript explicitly states that the abstract, methods, and results were written using a randomized Qualtrics dummy dataset rather than actual collected data. This makes all empirical findings, inferential tests, descriptive statistics, and conclusions invalid as evidence. A manuscript cannot be peer reviewed as an empirical replication if its results are simulated placeholders, unless clearly framed as a registered report/protocol with no inferential claims.
issues.quote: Results were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.

issues.subcategory: contradictory data-collection status
issues.description: The manuscript simultaneously says data collection was launched, completed before analyses, and that the results are based on randomized dummy data for preregistration. These statements are mutually inconsistent and obscure whether any real data exist, whether analyses were conducted after data collection, and whether preregistration preceded analysis.
issues.quote: Data collection for the experiment was launched at the start of the study period... All measures and manipulations conducted for this investigation are reported, and data collection was completed before analyses.

issues.subcategory: results reported as empirical despite dummy data
issues.description: The abstract reports substantive findings and hypotheses as supported even though the same section discloses the results are generated from dummy data. This is misleading and invalidates interpretation of the reported effects.
issues.quote: We generated a dummy set of samples in the Qualtrics survey (N = 1000) and found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect. To extend the replication... Results have supported the hypothesis...

issues.subcategory: self-selected experimental conditions
issues.description: The procedure states that participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions. This eliminates random assignment, introduces severe selection bias, and makes causal comparisons between conditions uninterpretable. It also contradicts the experimental framing and original design.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.subcategory: random assignment contradicted by self-selection
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly frames the study as an experiment with manipulated independent variables, but the procedure says participants selected their conditions. This contradiction affects the fundamental design and causal interpretability of all analyses.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.subcategory: within-subject design inconsistent with condition cell counts
issues.description: The manuscript describes the design as within-subject, but the tables show separate between-subject cell sizes summing to N=1000 across six cells. A within-subject design would require each participant to provide responses in multiple/all conditions and would require repeated-measures analyses. This ambiguity prevents evaluation of the design and invalidates the reported ANOVAs if the design was truly within-subject.
issues.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables

issues.subcategory: wrong analysis for within-subject design
issues.description: If the study is truly within-subject, the reported independent-groups two-way ANOVAs and independent t-tests are inappropriate because they ignore within-person dependence. Repeated-measures or mixed-effects models would be required. The residual df and cell counts suggest between-subject analyses, contradicting the stated design.
issues.quote: We conducted a 2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA to examine the effect of identifiability and intervention on donation.

issues.subcategory: major deviations from original replication
issues.description: The study changes several core features of the original experiments: real donations are replaced with hypothetical donations, laboratory recruitment is replaced with online MTurk, the original endowed money procedure is removed, updated stimuli are used, and Studies 1 and 3 are merged. These are not minor deviations and undermine the claim that this is a close or very close replication.
issues.quote: Imaginary donation Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.subcategory: hypothetical donation substituted for behavioral donation
issues.description: The original dependent variable was actual donation of endowed money. The replication uses imagined donation intentions, which may not capture actual costly prosocial behavior and is vulnerable to social desirability and hypothetical bias. This substantially changes the construct being measured.
issues.quote: Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.subcategory: removal of endowment procedure
issues.description: The original study endowed participants with five one-dollar bills earned from a survey before donation. The replication removes this procedure, changing the psychological ownership, windfall, and real-cost context of donation decisions. This can materially alter donation behavior.
issues.quote: No reward acquired from a pre-survey Participants will not conduct an irrelevant survey prior to the experiment to earn $5 for the donation

issues.subcategory: combining two original studies into one altered factorial design
issues.description: The replication merges Studies 1 and 3 and adds the explicit intervention to the joint condition. This creates a new 2 x 3 design not present in the original studies and changes the meaning of the joint/statistical comparison. The joint condition in Study 3 was intended as an implicit deliberation manipulation, whereas here it is crossed with explicit intervention, potentially confounding interpretation.
issues.quote: In this replication, we merged Studies 1 and 3 into one single experiment... The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition

issues.subcategory: joint condition construct changed
issues.description: The joint condition is interpreted as implicit learning or implicit deliberation, but adding explicit intervention to it changes the construct. A joint condition with explicit teaching is not equivalent to the original implicit manipulation and may reflect multiple overlapping manipulations.
issues.quote: The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition to reveal a more comprehensive comparison between the explicit and implicit settings.

issues.subcategory: intervention labeled learning despite different mechanisms
issues.description: The hypotheses describe the joint/statistics condition as 'implicitly learning' about the identifiable victim effect. In the original conceptualization, presenting statistical information may induce joint evaluation or deliberation; it is not necessarily learning about the effect. This mislabeling blurs the manipulation and theoretical mechanism.
issues.quote: implicitly learning about the effect would not be presented with such information but with the provision of victim statistics in the identifiable victim condition.

issues.subcategory: causal language unsupported under self-selection and dummy data
issues.description: The manuscript makes causal claims about deliberative thinking reducing donation, but if participants selected conditions and data are dummy-generated, neither experimental manipulation nor real empirical evidence supports causal inference.
issues.quote: Learning about the identifiable victim effect reduces people’s donation tendency

issues.subcategory: correlation described as prediction
issues.description: The manuscript uses correlation to examine whether feelings 'predict' donation. Cross-sectional correlations between concurrently measured self-reports and donation cannot establish prediction or directionality and are vulnerable to common-method and post-decision rationalization biases.
issues.quote: We conducted a correlation between aggregated feelings and donation to examine whether affective feelings predict donation.

issues.subcategory: incorrect or inconsistent direction of reported post-hoc effect
issues.description: The table reports Identifiable vs Statistical t = -2.40, but the narrative states statistical victims had higher donation. The descriptive table actually implies the identifiable mean across intervention/no-intervention cells is approximately 2.54 and statistical approximately 2.24, the opposite of the narrative. This suggests reversed labels, arithmetic error, or incorrect interpretation.
issues.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).

issues.subcategory: descriptive means do not match narrative means
issues.description: From Table 7, identifiable condition means are 2.58 and 2.50, whereas statistical condition means are 2.46 and 2.01. Collapsing across cells gives identifiable around 2.54 and statistical around 2.24. The narrative reverses these labels, saying statistical M=2.54 and identifiable M=2.24. This undermines trust in analysis and interpretation.
issues.quote: Table 7... Identifiable victim condition Intervention condition 2.58... No intervention condition 2.50... Statistical victim condition Intervention condition 2.46... No intervention condition 2.01

issues.subcategory: impossible/inconsistent t-test degrees of freedom for contrast
issues.description: Table 11 compares one condition (n=175) against all other conditions combined (n=825). An independent-samples t-test would have df = 998, but this comparison is highly unbalanced and not equivalent to the planned contrast within ANOVA unless handled with correct contrast coding. The table also lists the same df and t for both rows as if each group has df=998, which is poor/incomplete reporting.
issues.quote: Identifiable/ no intervention | 2.50 | 1.75 | 998 | 0.59... Other conditions | 2.42 | 1.67 | 998 | 0.59

issues.subcategory: inappropriate contrast changes original hypothesis
issues.description: The original contrast compared identifiable/no-intervention to three other conditions in a 2 x 2 design. The replication compares it to five conditions, including joint conditions that did not exist in Study 1. This alters the tested hypothesis and makes the replication contrast non-comparable to the original.
issues.quote: contrast the mean difference of identifiable/no intervention on donation with the combination of 5 conditions (statistical/no intervention, statistical/intervention, identifiable/intervention, joint/intervention, joint/no intervention)

issues.subcategory: ANOVA post-hoc tests reported with implausible effect sizes
issues.description: The post-hoc table reports t=-2.40 with d=0.076 and pBonferroni=.049. Given group means differ by about 0.30 and SDs around 1.7, d should be roughly 0.17-0.18, not 0.076. The reported d appears inconsistent with the mean difference and t statistic.

issues.subcategory: effect-size confidence interval incompatible with significance
issues.description: Table 10 reports a significant Bonferroni-adjusted p=.049 for Identifiable vs Statistical but gives a confidence interval for d that includes zero, [-0.05, 0.20]. Unless the CI is not adjusted or is for a different metric, this is inconsistent and requires clarification.

issues.subcategory: post-hoc means not reported or inconsistent
issues.description: The post-hoc tests do not report the condition means used for each comparison, and the narrative means are inconsistent with Table 7. This prevents independent verification of the tests.
issues.quote: Table 10 Summary of post-hoc tests for identifiability on donation

issues.subcategory: multiple testing not adequately controlled
issues.description: The manuscript tests many outcomes: donation, aggregated feelings, six segregated feelings, perceived impact, multiple interactions, post-hoc comparisons, and six correlations. Only some pairwise tests are Bonferroni-adjusted. There is no coherent family-wise or false-discovery control across the large set of exploratory/extension analyses, increasing false-positive risk.
issues.quote: Table 13 Summary of statistical tests for segregated feelings

issues.subcategory: post-hoc tests conditional on significance
issues.description: The analysis plan states that post-hoc contrasts are performed only if omnibus effects are significant. Conditional testing is common, but the manuscript inconsistently applies it and does not clearly specify all planned contrasts and correction families. This creates researcher degrees of freedom, especially with multiple outcomes.
issues.quote: Note: we conduct the test only if the interaction effect is significant

issues.subcategory: unclear preregistered primary outcome and analyses
issues.description: The study includes many hypotheses and analyses but does not clearly distinguish confirmatory preregistered tests from exploratory extensions or dummy-data scaffolding. It also states data collection was launched before the study period and completed before analyses, making preregistration timing unclear.
issues.quote: Power analyses and all materials used in these experiments are available in the supplementary materials.

issues.subcategory: power analysis details missing from manuscript
issues.description: The manuscript refers readers to supplementary materials for the power analysis but does not report the target effect size, alpha, desired power, allocation assumptions, exclusions, or achieved detectable effect. This prevents evaluation of whether N=1000 is justified, especially for interactions and condition-specific contrasts.
issues.quote: The full report of power analysis can be found in the supplementary under the section of “Power analysis of the original study effect”.

issues.subcategory: power based on main effect despite interaction hypothesis
issues.description: The evaluation criterion uses the original main effect of identifiability d=0.48, but key replication hypotheses concern the interaction between identifiability and intervention and the Study 3 joint-condition effect. Powering and evaluating the study on the wrong effect may be misleading.
issues.quote: We aim to study the effect of deliberative thinking on identifiable victim effect by comparing the replication effect with the original effect (d = 0.48, 95% CI [0.11, 0.84])

issues.subcategory: unclear effect-size conversion for original interactions
issues.description: The manuscript reports Cohen's d values for ANOVA main effects and interactions from the original studies without explaining the conversion method. Interactions in factorial ANOVA are not straightforwardly represented by a single d unless a specific contrast is defined. This affects replication evaluation and power calculations.
issues.quote: The interaction effect was d = 0.41, 95% CI [0.05, 0.77] when explicit learning was adopted to debias the identifiable victim effect.

issues.subcategory: original Study 3 df missing despite F statistic
issues.description: Table 2 reports Study 3 F=5.67 with df1=2 but df2=N/A. The denominator degrees of freedom are necessary to interpret the F statistic, compute p-values/effect sizes, and reproduce calculations. With N=159 and three groups, df2 would typically be 156 for a one-way ANOVA unless exclusions or a different model were used.
issues.quote: Identifiability Identifiable victim | 2 | N/A | 5.67 | <.01** | .07

issues.subcategory: ANOVA table incomplete denominator df reporting
issues.description: Tables 9, 12, and 13 report only effect df in the main rows and put residual df elsewhere. This is less transparent and can cause ambiguity. For F tests, both numerator and denominator degrees of freedom should be reported as F(df1, df2).

issues.subcategory: p-value and F rounding inconsistencies not verifiable
issues.description: The manuscript reports p-values and effect sizes without sums of squares, mean squares, or model specification. Given other inconsistencies, the inferential values cannot be verified or reproduced from the manuscript alone.
issues.quote: We conducted the data analysis with JAMOVI for statistical testing and R for calculation of 95%CI given that such function is not available for ANOVA testing in JAMOVI.

issues.subcategory: perceived-impact post-hoc effect inconsistent with CI
issues.description: Table 14 reports Statistical vs Joint pBonferroni=.041 but d=0.08 with CI [-0.07, 0.23], again a confidence interval including zero while the adjusted p is significant. This indicates inconsistency between test statistic, effect-size CI, and p-value or unclear CI metric.

issues.subcategory: extension hypothesis contradicted by reported result
issues.description: Hypothesis 6 predicts higher perceived impact for identifiable victims than statistical victims, but the reported significant post-hoc difference is between statistical and joint conditions, with statistical higher than joint. The abstract also states lower perceived impact for identifiable or joint conditions, which does not match the stated hypothesis.
issues.quote: An identifiable victim elicits higher perceived impact of donation than statistical victims

issues.subcategory: abstract conclusion inconsistent with hypothesis and results
issues.description: The abstract says people have lower perceived impact when facing an identifiable victim or identifiable victim with statistics, but the main reported post-hoc result only shows statistical > joint, and no significant identifiable vs statistical difference. This overstates and mischaracterizes the result.
issues.quote: Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.subcategory: ordinal donation scale analyzed as continuous without justification
issues.description: Donation appears bounded from $0 to $5, likely as discrete dollar amounts. The original used ordered probit in addition to ANOVA, but the replication drops ordered probit and uses ANOVA/t-tests without justifying assumptions for bounded ordinal/count-like outcomes. This may affect inference, especially with non-normal distributions and ceiling/floor effects.
issues.quote: Ordered probit regression... This test would not be conducted in the replication

issues.subcategory: bounded outcome not modeled appropriately
issues.description: The dependent variable is an imagined donation amount constrained to $0-$5. Linear ANOVA can be acceptable in some cases but should be justified or supplemented by robust/ordinal/beta-binomial-like approaches. No diagnostics or robustness checks are reported.
issues.quote: indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5

issues.subcategory: aggregated feelings scale not validated
issues.description: The manuscript aggregates heterogeneous items—upset, touched, sympathy, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and possibly perceived impact—without reporting reliability, dimensionality, scaling, or justification that they represent a single affective construct. Some items are moral/cognitive evaluations rather than affective feelings.
issues.quote: combine segregated feelings into one aggregated feeling

issues.subcategory: non-affective items labeled affective feelings
issues.description: The manuscript treats moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and perceived impact as affective feelings. These constructs are evaluative or efficacy beliefs, not emotions. Aggregating them with emotions compromises construct validity.
issues.quote: Segregated feelings include being upsetting, being touched, being sympathetic, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and perceived impact of donation

issues.subcategory: perceived impact operationalization unspecified
issues.description: The extension centers on perceived impact of donation, but the manuscript does not provide the actual item wording, response scale, timing, or whether it was measured before or after donation. Without this, construct validity and replicability cannot be assessed.
issues.quote: We aim to extend the replication study by considering the “perceived impact of donation” as one of the feeling variables

issues.subcategory: materials not included in manuscript
issues.description: Key stimuli, intervention text, victim descriptions, attention checks, exclusion questions, and feeling-item wording are not reported in the manuscript and are only linked externally. Links may not be permanent, and the manuscript itself lacks sufficient information for evaluation and replication.
issues.quote: For the full reported survey, please access the Qualtrics survey with the link below

issues.subcategory: sample source unclear/inconsistent
issues.description: The manuscript says responses were generated by Qualtrics for preregistration, but also describes recruitment from MTurk. It does not specify actual recruitment source, eligibility criteria, country restrictions, compensation, approval rates, or platform details.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration

issues.subcategory: Qualtrics-generated responses vs MTurk participants
issues.description: The participant section describes Qualtrics generated responses, while the design-deviation table says MTurk workers will be recruited. These are different sources and imply different data-generating processes.
issues.quote: MTurk workers as participants We will recruit participants on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform

issues.subcategory: exclusion counts missing
issues.description: The manuscript states participants with prior knowledge or failed attention checks were excluded but does not report how many were excluded, whether exclusions were preregistered, whether N=1000 is before or after exclusions, or exclusion criteria wording.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.subcategory: missing data handling absent
issues.description: There is no description of missing data, incomplete surveys, dropout, item nonresponse, or how missing values were handled in analyses. This is essential for online studies and especially for multi-condition designs.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.subcategory: attrition not reported
issues.description: The manuscript does not report the number of participants who began the survey, completed it, were excluded, or remained for each analysis. Cell sizes are reported but without a CONSORT-like flow or explanation of unequal cells.
issues.quote: Table 7 Descriptive statistics for donation across conditions

issues.subcategory: unequal cell sizes unexplained
issues.description: The six cell sizes are unequal despite an ostensibly factorial design. If random assignment was used, the randomization method and imbalance should be described; if participants selected conditions, the imbalance reflects selection bias. No explanation is provided.

issues.subcategory: manipulation checks absent
issues.description: The study relies on learning about the identifiable victim effect and implicit deliberation through joint presentation, but no manipulation checks are reported to verify participants read, understood, or engaged in deliberative/analytic thinking.
issues.quote: Learning about the identifiable victim effect reduces people’s donation tendency

issues.subcategory: deliberative thinking not directly measured
issues.description: The core theoretical claim concerns deliberative or analytical reasoning, yet the study only manipulates information exposure and does not assess whether analytical reasoning was actually induced. This weakens construct validity of the independent variable.
issues.quote: thinking analytically about your helping behaviour would reduce your motivation to offer assistance to a single beneficiary

issues.subcategory: demand characteristics from explicit teaching
issues.description: Explicitly teaching participants about the identifiable victim effect before asking for donations may create demand characteristics or social desirability pressures rather than genuine deliberative reasoning. The manuscript does not address this alternative explanation or include controls to separate awareness from demand.
issues.quote: participants under manipulation were taught about the identifiable victim effect before donating to the victims

issues.subcategory: no blinding or hypothesis masking reported
issues.description: No information is provided about whether participants were blinded to hypotheses, whether experimenter interaction existed, or how demand effects were minimized. This matters because the intervention explicitly reveals the bias under study.
issues.quote: one group learning about the identifiable victim effect from previous research while another served as a control group

issues.subcategory: attention check unspecified
issues.description: The manuscript mentions an attention check but does not provide its wording, placement, exclusion threshold, or whether failure was independent of condition. Exclusions based on attention checks can bias results if not transparently reported.
issues.quote: those who failed the attention check

issues.subcategory: sample age implausible and unrepresentative
issues.description: The reported sample has a mean age of 67.8, SD 30.1, and range 18-120, which is highly unusual for MTurk and may reflect dummy data or poor data quality. The manuscript does not discuss implications for generalizability or data validity.

issues.subcategory: demographics insufficient
issues.description: The manuscript reports only gender and age, and even geographic origin is unspecified. For a charitable-donation study involving African famine victims, location, nationality, socioeconomic status, income, religiosity, prior charitable giving, and cultural context may be relevant to interpret generalizability.
issues.quote: Geographic origin | Not specified

issues.subcategory: contextual shift from university lab to MTurk not adequately addressed
issues.description: The original sample was recruited in a university student center and made real donations from endowed cash; the replication uses an online MTurk setting with hypothetical donations. These contextual differences likely affect behavior and limit comparability, but the manuscript still calls the study close to very close.
issues.quote: Online survey Participants will conduct an online survey in Qualtrics on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform while the original study surveyed inside a student center of a university in Pennsylvania

issues.subcategory: overclaiming classic phenomenon from altered sample and procedure
issues.description: The manuscript aims to draw conclusions about the identifiable victim effect broadly, but the sample, hypothetical online task, and altered stimuli limit generalizability. These limitations are not sufficiently acknowledged.
issues.quote: We aim to revisit the classic phenomenon to examine the reproducibility and replicability of the findings with independent replications.

issues.subcategory: classification table inconsistent with stated deviations
issues.description: The manuscript labels the replication 'close to very close' even though DV stimuli are listed as different, physical settings different, contextual variables different, and several core procedural details changed. This contradicts the Lebel framework table shown immediately above.
issues.quote: Replication classification | close to very close replication

issues.subcategory: updated victim information may alter stimulus equivalence
issues.description: Using updated victim information from Save the Children may change severity, emotional vividness, cultural cues, credibility, and perceived need. Without reporting and validating equivalence to the original stimuli, stimulus changes threaten comparability.
issues.quote: We will present the participants with the most updated victim information retrieved from the website of Save the Children given that those used in the original study was dated two decades ago.

issues.subcategory: identifiability confounded with singularity and vividness
issues.description: The identifiable victim condition appears to involve a named/described single African girl, whereas the statistical condition involves starvation statistics. This confounds identifiability with number of victims, vividness, narrative detail, and concreteness. The manuscript discusses these factors but does not control them, limiting interpretation of the identifiable victim effect.
issues.quote: information either about the problem of starvation in Africa or a brief description of an African girl retrieved from the website of Save the Children

issues.subcategory: overstatement of identifiable victim effect definition
issues.description: The identifiable victim effect is described as giving more to a specific victim than to a group of statistical individuals, but the literature often distinguishes identifiability, singularity, proportion dominance, and reference group effects. The manuscript sometimes conflates these mechanisms, creating conceptual ambiguity.
issues.quote: The identifiable victim effect is a phenomenon characterized by the human’s tendency to give out more aid to a specific victim than to a group of statistical individuals.

issues.subcategory: misapplied availability heuristic explanation
issues.description: The manuscript attributes stronger responses to identifiable victims to the availability heuristic, but the explanation given is more about vividness, affect, concreteness, and sympathy than availability as frequency/probability judgment based on retrieval ease. This conceptual imprecision weakens the theoretical framing.
issues.quote: The “availability heuristic”... is believed to be activated when we value a personalized individual... The information we receive about this person may elicit stronger affective reactions such as sympathy and distress

issues.subcategory: normative claims unsupported
issues.description: The introduction claims donations to identifiable victims reflect unfairness and inefficient resource allocation, but the study does not measure fairness, efficiency, cost-effectiveness, or social welfare. These claims go beyond the empirical design.
issues.quote: The inconsistent prosocial motivation not only demonstrates human sense of unfairness in valuing life, but also highlights the lack of efficiency in resource allocation

issues.subcategory: compensation missing
issues.description: Compensation is unspecified for the replication. Compensation can affect attention, selection, and donation decisions, especially when the original design involved a $5 endowment.
issues.quote: Compensation | US$5 | Not specified

issues.subcategory: no real incentive compatibility
issues.description: Because participants are not actually donating earned money, the task lacks incentive compatibility. This is especially problematic because the original study's outcome was actual giving behavior.
issues.quote: Imaginary donation

issues.subcategory: survey timing/order not reported
issues.description: The manuscript does not clearly specify the order of intervention, victim information, donation decision, manipulation checks, affective measures, attention checks, and demographics. Order matters because affect measures after donation may reflect justification rather than antecedent emotion.
issues.quote: The session of “Procedure” in the supplementary summarizes the procedure of the current replication study.

issues.subcategory: post-donation feelings may not measure decision antecedents
issues.description: The original and replication appear to measure affective feelings after donation. If these are interpreted as mechanisms influencing donation, post-decision measurement cannot distinguish cause from consequence or rationalization.
issues.quote: After the donation, they had to fill up a questionnaire for different cognitive evaluations they experienced which may influence their choice of donation.

issues.subcategory: mediation implied without mediation analysis
issues.description: The extension motivates perceived impact as a mediator or explanatory factor, but the analyses only test mean differences and do not conduct mediation or causal pathway analyses. Claims about being linked to or accounting for the identifiable victim effect are therefore unsupported.
issues.quote: there were mixed findings regarding the mediation effect of perceived impact on the identifiable victim effect

issues.subcategory: correlation analyses underpowered within cells not justified
issues.description: Although total N is 1000, cell-specific correlations have n around 159-175. No power analysis is reported for correlations within six conditions, and multiple comparisons further reduce power. Null correlations are interpreted as contrary to original without equivalence testing or sensitivity analysis.
issues.quote: correlation between aggregated feelings and donation across six different conditions

issues.subcategory: no equivalence or non-inferiority tests for null claims
issues.description: The manuscript concludes no empirical support for analytical reasoning effects based on non-significant tests. Failure to reject the null is not evidence of no effect unless equivalence tests, Bayes factors, or confidence intervals relative to smallest effect sizes of interest are provided.
issues.quote: found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect

issues.subcategory: replication evaluation framework not actually applied
issues.description: The manuscript says it will use LeBel et al. criteria comparing replication effect sizes and confidence intervals to original effects, but the results do not present a formal classification of the replication outcome using those criteria.
issues.quote: using the criteria set by Lebel, Vanpaemel, Cheung, and Campbell (2019)

issues.subcategory: table numbering errors
issues.description: The manuscript references Table 7 as summarizing replication classification, but the classification table is labeled Table 6 and Table 7 is descriptive donation statistics. Such inconsistencies impede readability and replication tracking.
issues.quote: Table 7 summarizes the current replication as a "close to very close replication".

issues.subcategory: duplicate table columns and malformed tables
issues.description: Several tables have duplicated columns or malformed headers, such as Table 4 with two identical replication columns and Table 5 with repeated 'Hypothetical effect'. This makes reporting confusing and increases risk of misinterpretation.
issues.quote: Sample size | Study 1: 121 Study 3: 159 | 1000 | 1000

issues.subcategory: ethics approval and consent missing
issues.description: The manuscript does not report institutional review board/ethics approval, informed consent, debriefing, or participant rights. This is required for human-subjects research, especially involving deception/demand and donation decisions.
issues.quote: Participants

issues.subcategory: prior knowledge exclusion may induce post-treatment bias if measured after manipulation
issues.description: Participants with prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect are excluded, but the timing of this question is not specified. If assessed after the intervention, participants in the intervention condition may endorse knowledge because they just learned about it, producing differential exclusion bias.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded

issues.subcategory: randomization procedure absent
issues.description: Despite experimental language, no randomization method, allocation ratio, block/randomizer settings, or concealment procedure is described. This is essential for evaluating internal validity.
issues.quote: The experimental design can be retrieved from the supplementary under the section of “Table of design”.

issues.subcategory: condition preference selection contaminates manipulation
issues.description: If participants choose conditions, their preferences may be associated with generosity, attitudes toward charity, numeracy, skepticism, or emotional responsiveness. This confounds condition effects with participant characteristics.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.subcategory: no demographic balance checks
issues.description: Given unequal cells and possible self-selection, the manuscript should report condition balance on demographics and relevant covariates. No such checks are provided.
issues.quote: Table 4 is a comparison of samples from the target article and the replication.

issues.subcategory: no model diagnostics or assumption checks
issues.description: ANOVA assumptions such as independence, homogeneity of variances, residual distribution, and robustness for bounded outcomes are not assessed or reported. This is important given online data, unequal cell sizes, and bounded donation responses.
issues.quote: We conducted a 2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA

issues.subcategory: software versions missing
issues.description: The manuscript mentions JAMOVI and R but does not report versions, packages, functions, or exact code outputs in the manuscript. This limits computational reproducibility.
issues.quote: We conducted the data analysis with JAMOVI for statistical testing and R for calculation of 95%CI

issues.subcategory: external supplement required for key analytic decisions
issues.description: Critical details including power analysis, experimental design, procedure, comparisons, deviations, and open-science disclosures are deferred to external documents. Reliance on mutable Google Docs/Dropbox links rather than complete manuscript reporting creates transparency and reproducibility risks.
issues.quote: Full open-science details and disclosures are provided in the supplementary.

issues.subcategory: dead placeholder links
issues.description: Some project links are placeholders rather than actual materials. This undermines claims of open materials and reviewability.
issues.quote: Cloud folder for presentation (PPT and PDF) | <enter link here> Cloud folder for peer reviews | <enter link here>

issues.subcategory: misuse of debiasing terminology
issues.description: The manuscript describes reduced donations to identifiable victims as 'debiasing', but whether reducing aid to an identifiable victim is normatively better depends on goals and comparative cost-effectiveness. The study does not establish bias correction versus reduced sympathy/callousness.
issues.quote: debiasing the identifiable victim effect through inducing a calculative thinking mechanism

issues.subcategory: intervention may reduce giving generally rather than debias identifiability
issues.description: Hypothesis 2 predicts a main effect of learning that reduces donation tendency overall. Such an effect would not specifically show debiasing of the identifiable victim effect; it could reflect generalized cynicism, demand, or reduced emotional engagement. The design and interpretation need to separate general donation suppression from interaction-specific debiasing.
issues.quote: Learning about the identifiable victim effect reduces people’s donation tendency

issues.subcategory: main effect hypothesis conflicts with original interaction focus
issues.description: The manuscript states Hypothesis 2 as a main effect that learning reduces donation, but the original theory predicts learning reduces giving to identifiable victims but not statistical victims. A main effect may be theoretically ambiguous and could contradict the debiasing account.
issues.quote: thinking analytically about the value of lives reduces giving to an identifiable victim but not to statistical victims

issues.subcategory: Bonferroni post-hoc after significant interaction not targeted
issues.description: After a significant interaction, the manuscript reports main-effect post-hoc comparisons for identifiability collapsed across intervention. Collapsing across a significant interaction can be misleading; simple effects or planned interaction contrasts should be tested instead.
issues.quote: To further deduce the particular conditions in resulting the above significant findings, we performed post-hoc tests for the difference of identifiability on donation.

issues.subcategory: planned interaction contrast not appropriate for six-cell design
issues.description: The reported follow-up for the significant interaction compares identifiable/no-intervention against the average of all other five cells. This does not directly test whether explicit learning selectively reduces donation to identifiable victims but not statistical victims, nor whether joint presentation reduces identifiable giving. More specific simple-effect contrasts are required.

issues.subcategory: claims of support based on marginal small effect

issues.quote: It is hypothesized that people generally perceive a stronger impact of donation towards an identified victim than unidentified statistical victims.

issues.subcategory: original-study extraction methods insufficient
issues.description: The manuscript reports recalculated original effect sizes but does not explain whether they were based on means/SDs, F values, assumed equal cell sizes, or extracted from tables. This matters for power and replication comparison.

issues.subcategory: author contribution inconsistency

issues.quote: Role | Yik Chun Wong | Gilad Feldman | So Chi Liu

issues.subcategory: no preregistration timestamp or deviations summarized
issues.description: The manuscript provides an OSF link but does not report the preregistration date relative to data collection, whether registration was frozen, or a transparent list of deviations from preregistered analyses. issues.quote: Pre-registration on the Open Science Framework | <https://osf.io/n4jkh/?view_only=d52771c7540a4a8f8051c8b430a6f15d>

issues.subcategory: dummy data before final analyses can enable undisclosed analytic tuning
issues.description: Writing and testing the full analysis pipeline on dummy data is not inherently wrong, but if dummy data are used to develop reporting decisions, contrasts, and interpretation language without a fixed analysis plan, it may introduce analytic flexibility. The manuscript does not clearly separate preregistered planned analyses from template results.
issues.quote: Method and results sections were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection.

issues.subcategory: no control for charitable attitudes or prior donation behavior
issues.description: Donation behavior may vary by income, charitable orientation, familiarity with Save the Children, political ideology, religiosity, and empathy. issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.subcategory: Save the Children trustworthiness not controlled despite being measured originally
issues.description: The original study measured trustworthiness, accountability, organizational efficiency, and appropriateness. issues.quote: These items included beliefs about the severity of the crisis, the perceived trustworthiness of the charity, the expected accountability of funds, evaluation of organizational efficiency, and the appropriateness of donation to help the victims.

issues.subcategory: dependent-variable timing and target unclear in joint condition
issues.description: In the joint condition, participants receive both identifiable and statistical victim information, but it is unclear whether donation is directed to the identifiable victim, the statistical victims, Save the Children generally, or both. issues.quote: The third group was considered as a joint condition provided with both statistical and identifiable victim information.

issues.subcategory: donation target ambiguity in joint condition

issues.quote: indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s)

issues.subcategory: collapsing across joint condition changes main effect of identifiability

issues.quote: effect of identifiability on donation (with joint condition)

issues.subcategory: original vs replication comparison confounds study 1 and study 3
issues.description: Table 9 compares original Study 1 two-way ANOVA effects with a replication 2 x 3 ANOVA that includes the joint condition from Study 3. These are not equivalent models, so direct comparison is misleading.
issues.quote: Original study | 1 | 6.75... Replication | 2 | 3.58

issues.subcategory: inadequate handling of interaction with three-level factor
issues.description: The significant 2 x 3 interaction is not decomposed into theoretically relevant components: explicit intervention effect within identifiable, statistical, and joint conditions; identifiable vs statistical difference within intervention levels; and joint vs identifiable comparisons. issues.quote: Results from Table 9 showed that... the interaction effect of identifiability and intervention was supported.

issues.subcategory: no figures shown despite references
issues.description: The manuscript references Figures 1-4, but the provided text does not include actual figures. Missing figures prevent review of distributions, replication evaluation taxonomy, and visual diagnostics.
issues.quote: Figure 3. A violin plot with jittered data for the main effect of identifiability on donation.

issues.subcategory: cultural context not addressed
issues.description: The authors are based in Hong Kong, the original study was US-based, and the intended platform is MTurk, but participant geography is unspecified. issues.quote: Geographic origin | US American | Not specified | Not specified

issues.subcategory: online unattended setting may reduce stimulus engagement
issues.description: Moving from a lab/student-center setting with physical cash and charity forms to an online survey may reduce engagement and emotional impact. No design features are reported to ensure attentive reading beyond an unspecified attention check.
issues.quote: Physical settings | Different | Online survey Participants will conduct an online survey in Qualtrics

issues.subcategory: use of p<.05 labels for original exact p unavailable
issues.description: Original p-values are reported only as thresholds, which may be unavoidable from the original article, but the manuscript uses them in comparisons without reporting exact values or explaining limitations. This limits precise replication evaluation.
issues.quote: Original study | 1 | 6.75 | <.05*

issues.subcategory: no data-quality screening for bots/duplicate MTurk responses

issues.subcategory: SD notation ambiguous

issues.subcategory: affective heuristic framework inconsistently linked to perceived impact
